claim: TIS granule network shares a large surface area with the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
source: One such condensate is the TIS granule network that shares a large surface area with the rough endoplasmic reticulum and is important for membrane protein trafficking.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract as a characteristic of TIS granules

claim: TIS granule network is important for membrane protein trafficking.
source: One such condensate is the TIS granule network that shares a large surface area with the rough endoplasmic reticulum and is important for membrane protein trafficking.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract and supported by previous work

claim: The minimal components for mesh-like condensate formation are a multivalent RNA-binding protein that concentrates RNAs able to form extensive intermolecular mRNA–mRNA interactions.
source: In vitro and in vivo reconstitution experiments revealed that the minimal components are a multivalent RNA-binding protein that concentrates RNAs that are able to form extensive intermolecular mRNA–mRNA interactions.
evidence: Conclusion from in vitro and in vivo reconstitution experiments described in the manuscript

claim: mRNAs with large unstructured regions have a high propensity to form a pervasive intermolecular interaction network that acts as condensate skeleton.
source: mRNAs with large unstructured regions have a high propensity to form a pervasive intermolecular interaction network that acts as condensate skeleton.
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript

claim: The underlying RNA matrix prevents full fusion of spherical liquid-like condensates, thus driving the formation of irregularly shaped membraneless organelles.
source: The underlying RNA matrix prevents full fusion of spherical liquid-like condensates, thus driving the formation of irregularly shaped membraneless organelles.
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by fusion experiments and imaging data

claim: The large surface area of mesh-like condensates may promote interactions at the condensate surface and at the interface with other organelles.
source: The resulting large surface area may promote interactions at the condensate surface and at the interface with other organelles.
evidence: Stated in abstract as a potential functional consequence

claim: Most known membraneless organelles are spherical and include stress granules, P granules, and the nucleolus.
source: Most known membraneless organelles are spherical and include stress granules, P granules, and the nucleolus (Seydoux and Fire, 1994; Kedersha et al., 1999; Brangwynne et al., 2009; Brangwynne et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Several mesh-like condensates were found in cells that include the TIS granule network, FXR1 condensates, and localization bodies (L-bodies).
source: Recently, several mesh-like condensates were found in cells that include the TIS granule network, FXR1 condensates, and localization bodies (L-bodies) (Ma and Mayr, 2018; Neil et al., 2020; Smith et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: TIS granules are formed through assembly of the RNA-binding protein TIS11B.
source: TIS granules are formed through assembly of the RNA-binding protein TIS11B.
evidence: Stated directly in the introduction

claim: TIS granules have tubule-like structures and generate a reticular meshwork that is intertwined with the rough endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: TIS granules have tubule-like structures and generate a reticular meshwork that is intertwined with the rough endoplasmic reticulum (ER), one of the major sites of protein translation.
evidence: Stated directly in the introduction

claim: TIS granules are present in various cell types under physiological conditions.
source: TIS granules are present in various cell types under physiological conditions and provide a translation environment for mRNAs that contain several AU-rich elements in their 3′ untranslated regions (3′UTRs).
evidence: Stated directly in the introduction

claim: TIS granules provide a translation environment for mRNAs that contain several AU-rich elements in their 3′UTRs.
source: TIS granules are present in various cell types under physiological conditions and provide a translation environment for mRNAs that contain several AU-rich elements in their 3′ untranslated regions (3′UTRs).
evidence: Stated directly in the introduction

claim: Translation in the TIGER domain allows membrane proteins to form specific protein complexes.
source: Translation in the TIS granule–ER interface, the so-called TIGER domain, allows membrane proteins to form specific protein complexes, indicating that TIS granules are important for the trafficking of plasma membrane proteins (Ma and Mayr, 2018; Mayr, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: L-bodies localize to the vegetal pole in Xenopus oocytes and have a mesh-like shape.
source: Condensates that contain Vg1 mRNA and several RNA-binding proteins, including Vera, were recently discovered in frog oocytes. These so-called L-bodies localize to the vegetal pole and have a mesh-like shape (Neil et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: TIS granules share a lot of characteristics with L-bodies.
source: Although TIS granules were found in somatic cells, they seem to share a lot of characteristics with L-bodies.
evidence: Stated as an inference based on comparison

claim: Many biomolecular condensates or RNA granules contain protein and RNA.
source: Many biomolecular condensates or RNA granules contain protein and RNA (Teixeira et al., 2005; Schwartz et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2016; Banerjee et al., 2017; Fuller et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2020; Fernandes and Buchan, 2020; Hyman et al., 2014; Banani et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Both protein and RNA components contribute to the multivalency of phase separation systems.
source: It is well established that both components contribute to the multivalency of phase separation systems.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: RNA can phase separate without protein.
source: Through use of RNA, including total RNA (Van Treeck and Parker, 2018), RNA with repeats (Jain and Vale, 2017), artificial RNAs (Lin et al., 2015; Ries et al., 2019) or homopolymers (Elbaum-Garfinkle et al., 2015; Wei et al., 2017; Boeynaems et al., 2019), and a handful of mRNAs, it has been demonstrated that RNA can phase separate without protein and that RNA can promote or inhibit phase separation (Jain and Vale, 2017; Maharana et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: RNA can promote or inhibit phase separation.
source: Through use of RNA, including total RNA (Van Treeck and Parker, 2018), RNA with repeats (Jain and Vale, 2017), artificial RNAs (Lin et al., 2015; Ries et al., 2019) or homopolymers (Elbaum-Garfinkle et al., 2015; Wei et al., 2017; Boeynaems et al., 2019), and a handful of mRNAs, it has been demonstrated that RNA can phase separate without protein and that RNA can promote or inhibit phase separation (Jain and Vale, 2017; Maharana et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Protein–RNA interactions can influence the identity and material properties of condensates in vitro and in vivo.
source: It has also been shown that protein–RNA interactions can influence the identity and material properties of condensates in vitro and in vivo (Elbaum-Garfinkle et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015; Langdon et al., 2018; Boeynaems et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: It is currently unknown how different RNAs influence various aspects of phase separation.
source: However, as RNA is not a uniform entity, it is currently unknown how different RNAs influence various aspects of phase separation (Van Treeck and Parker, 2018; Jain and Vale, 2017; Lin et al., 2015; Ries et al., 2019; Elbaum-Garfinkle et al., 2015; Wei et al., 2017; Boeynaems et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2015; Langdon et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated as a knowledge gap in the field

claim: Spherical condensates are liquid-like.
source: Early on, it was established that spherical condensates are liquid-like (Brangwynne et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Different phase separation systems can have a wide range of material properties ranging from liquid-like to gel-like to solid.
source: Moreover, different phase separation systems can have a wide range of material properties ranging from liquid-like to gel-like to solid (Alberti et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Surface tension promotes sphere formation of liquid droplets.
source: Surface tension promotes sphere formation of liquid droplets (Hyman et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Non-spherical and irregularly shaped condensates are widely accepted to be aggregates and must be gel-like or solid.
source: This led to the widely accepted conclusion that non-spherical and irregularly shaped condensates are aggregates and must be gel-like or solid (Molliex et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2015; Qamar et al., 2018; Boeynaems et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature describing the prevailing view

claim: The authors observed condensates with mesh-like or filamentous morphology, but with dynamic protein components.
source: In the course of our studies, we made the intriguing and, at first glance, paradoxical observation of condensates with mesh-like or filamentous morphology, but with dynamic protein components.
evidence: Stated as an observation from the authors' studies

claim: The three-dimensional organization of mesh-like condensates is determined by RNA.
source: We used chimeric RNA-binding proteins as models to study how the three-dimensional organization of mesh-like condensates is controlled and found that it is determined by RNA.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the authors' experiments

claim: The addition of predominantly structured mRNAs generated spherical condensates.
source: We examined the influence of 47 human in vitro transcribed 3′UTRs on phase separation behavior of an RNA-binding protein. Whereas the addition of predominantly structured mRNAs generated spherical condensates, the addition of largely unstructured mRNAs induced formation of mesh-like condensates.
evidence: Stated as a result from examining 47 3'UTRs

claim: The addition of largely unstructured mRNAs induced formation of mesh-like condensates.
source: We examined the influence of 47 human in vitro transcribed 3′UTRs on phase separation behavior of an RNA-binding protein. Whereas the addition of predominantly structured mRNAs generated spherical condensates, the addition of largely unstructured mRNAs induced formation of mesh-like condensates.
evidence: Stated as a result from examining 47 3'UTRs

claim: Transfected TIS granules largely recapitulated the mesh-like three-dimensional structure of endogenous TIS granules.
source: When we initially discovered TIS granules, we expressed mCherry-tagged TIS11B in HeLa cells and observed that the transfected TIS granules largely recapitulated the mesh-like three-dimensional structure of endogenous TIS granules (Figure 1A).
evidence: Stated observation supported by Figure 1A showing confocal imaging

claim: TIS granules showed 20% fluorescence recovery in 120 s at 16 hr after transfection.
source: At the time, we performed fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) after 16 hr of transfection and observed 20% of fluorescence recovery in 120 s (Ma and Mayr, 2018).
evidence: Stated as a previous observation with citation

claim: TIS granules showed 43% fluorescent recovery in 10 s at 5 hr after transfection.
source: More recently, we repeated the FRAP experiment at 5 hr after transfection and observed 43% fluorescent recovery of GFP-tagged TIS11B in 10 s (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Stated observation supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: TIS granules generated from transfected constructs have somewhat dynamic protein components at 5 hr after transfection despite being irregularly shaped.
source: This observation suggested that at this time point TIS granules generated from transfected constructs have somewhat dynamic protein components despite being irregularly shaped.
evidence: Inference from FRAP data

claim: L-bodies in frog oocytes have a mesh-like morphology but dynamic protein components.
source: This observation is reminiscent of L-bodies in frog oocytes, which have a mesh-like morphology but dynamic protein components (Neil et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The material properties of endogenous TIS granules are currently unknown.
source: It is important to point out that the material properties of endogenous TIS granules are currently unknown as all experiments so far have been performed with fluorescently tagged TIS11B constructs (Ma and Mayr, 2018).
evidence: Stated as a limitation of current knowledge

claim: Point mutations that disrupt RNA binding in TIS11B turn mesh-like assemblies into sphere-like condensates that are no longer intertwined with the ER.
source: When we introduced different point mutations to disrupt RNA binding (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C; Lai et al., 2000), the mesh-like assemblies were turned into sphere-like condensates that are no longer intertwined with the ER (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: Stated observation supported by figures showing mutant constructs

claim: The mesh-like organization of TIS granules requires the recruitment of mRNAs.
source: This suggested that the mesh-like organization of TIS granules requires the recruitment of mRNAs.
evidence: Inference from RNA-binding mutant experiments

claim: Expression of the TIS11B RBD alone is not sufficient for condensate formation.
source: Expression of the TIS11B RBD alone is not sufficient for condensate formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Stated observation supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: SUMO-SIM-TIS generates filamentous condensates that are not intertwined with the ER.
source: However, when we fused SUMO-SIM to the TIS11B RBD (SUMO-SIM-TIS), we observed a filamentous condensate that is not intertwined with the ER (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Stated observation supported by figures

claim: Intertwinement with the ER is not necessary for mesh-like condensate formation.
source: This was an important result as it demonstrates that intertwinement with the ER is not necessary for mesh-like condensate formation.
evidence: Inference from SUMO-SIM-TIS experiment

claim: Expression of the FUS-IDR alone did not generate condensates.
source: Expression of the FUS-IDR alone did not generate condensates (Figure 1D).
evidence: Stated observation supported by Figure 1D

claim: FUS-TIS generates cytoplasmic mesh-like condensates that look very similar to wild-type TIS granules.
source: When we fused the RBD of TIS11B to the IDR of FUS to generate FUS TIS, we observed cytoplasmic mesh-like condensates that look very similar to wild-type TIS granules (Figure 1D).
evidence: Stated observation supported by Figure 1D

claim: In the context of FUS-TIS, the RBD of TIS11B is functional as it recruits the same mRNAs to the condensates.
source: In the context of FUS-TIS, the RBD of TIS11B is functional as it recruits the same mRNAs to the condensates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Stated observation supported by RNA-FISH data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C

claim: Both FUS-TIS and SUMO-SIM-TIS show fast fluorescence recovery in FRAP experiments.
source: Importantly, both FUS-TIS and SUMO-SIM-TIS show fast fluorescence recovery in FRAP experiments (Figure 1E), indicating that the filamentous networks have highly mobile protein components and are not aggregates.
evidence: Stated observation supported by Figure 1E showing FRAP data

claim: The filamentous networks formed by FUS-TIS and SUMO-SIM-TIS have highly mobile protein components and are not aggregates.
source: Importantly, both FUS-TIS and SUMO-SIM-TIS show fast fluorescence recovery in FRAP experiments (Figure 1E), indicating that the filamentous networks have highly mobile protein components and are not aggregates.
evidence: Inference from FRAP data in Figure 1E

claim: In the context of various multivalent domains the TIS11B RBD generates mesh-like condensates in vivo.
source: These experiments reveal that in the context of various multivalent domains the TIS11B RBD generates mesh-like condensates in vivo.
evidence: Summary of experiments with different chimeric proteins

claim: FUS-TIS phase separates into sphere-like condensates that are liquid-like.
source: FUS-TIS phase separates into sphere-like condensates that are liquid-like (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: Stated observation supported by figures showing phase separation and fusion

claim: The addition of the FUS 3′UTR did not change the morphology of the sphere-like condensates formed by FUS-TIS.
source: The addition of the FUS 3′UTR did not change the morphology of the sphere-like condensates formed by FUS-TIS (Figure 2A).
evidence: Stated observation supported by Figure 2A

claim: Addition of 3′UTRs of TIS11B target mRNAs (CD47, CD274, ELAVL1) resulted in formation of mesh-like FUS-TIS condensates.
source: However, when we added 3′UTRs of TIS11B target mRNAs, including CD47, CD274 (PD-L1) or ELAVL1 (HuR) (Ma and Mayr, 2018), we observed formation of mesh-like FUS-TIS condensates (Figure 2A).
evidence: Stated observation supported by Figure 2A

claim: The mesh-like condensates formed by FUS-TIS with CD47 3'UTR do not represent aggregates as FUS-TIS protein showed fast fluorescence recovery in FRAP experiments at 2 and 16 hr.
source: Importantly, the mesh-like condensates do not represent aggregates as FUS-TIS protein showed fast fluorescence recovery in FRAP experiments performed at 2 and 16 hr after induction of phase separation (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Stated observation supported by FRAP data in figures

claim: Network formation was already observed at the early time point (2 hr), but longer incubation led to formation of a more extensive network.
source: Network formation was already observed at the early time point, but longer incubation led to formation of a more extensive network (Figure 2A, C, Figure 2—figure supplements 1G and 2A–D).
evidence: Stated observation supported by time-course imaging data

claim: The capacity for network formation is an intrinsic property of the RNA as sphere-forming RNAs did not form networks even at high concentrations.
source: Although the minimum RNA concentration required to induce network formation varied, these experiments revealed that the capacity for network formation is an intrinsic property of the RNA as sphere-forming RNAs did not form networks even at high concentrations.
evidence: Inference from concentration-dependent experiments

claim: At high RNA concentrations, inhibition of phase separation was often observed.
source: Instead, at high RNA concentrations, we often observed inhibition of phase separation, as was observed previously (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G; Maharana et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated observation supported by figures and citation

claim: Network formation is not only determined by the length of the RNA.
source: All longer RNAs formed networks, but we observed both network and sphere formation for RNAs shorter than 2000 nt, indicating that network formation is not only determined by the length of the RNA (Figures 2D and 3A, Figure 3—figure supplements 1A–C and 2A, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Stated conclusion from testing 19 additional RNAs of varying lengths

claim: High concentrations of RNAs alone without the addition of FUS-TIS protein did not result in phase separation.
source: We did not observe phase separation when using high concentrations of the RNAs alone without the addition of FUS-TIS protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Stated observation supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2B

claim: The number of AU-rich elements in sphere- and network-forming RNAs with a length shorter than 2000 nt is not significantly different.
source: Within this size-restricted cohort, the number of AU-rich elements or the GC-content of the RNA had no influence on network formation (Figure 3B, C).
evidence: Stated observation supported by Figure 3B showing no significant difference

claim: The GC-content of sphere- and network-forming RNAs with a length shorter than 2000 nt is not significantly different.
source: Within this size-restricted cohort, the number of AU-rich elements or the GC-content of the RNA had no influence on network formation (Figure 3B, C).
evidence: Stated observation supported by Figure 3C showing no significant difference

claim: There is a strong association between the propensity of an RNA to induce network formation and the predicted 'unstructured-ness' of the RNA.
source: We observed a strong association between the propensity of an RNA to induce network formation and the predicted 'unstructured-ness' of the RNA.
evidence: Stated observation from RNAfold structure predictions

claim: For sphere-inducing RNAs, the majority of their nucleotides are predicted to form strong local structures.
source: For sphere-inducing RNAs, the majority of their nucleotides are predicted to form strong local structures, whereas RNAs with a high propensity for network formation are predicted to contain large, unstructured regions (Figure 3D, E, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–D, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Stated observation from RNAfold predictions shown in figures

claim: RNAs with a high propensity for network formation are predicted to contain large, unstructured regions.
source: For sphere-inducing RNAs, the majority of their nucleotides are predicted to form strong local structures, whereas RNAs with a high propensity for network formation are predicted to contain large, unstructured regions (Figure 3D, E, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–D, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Stated observation from RNAfold predictions shown in figures

claim: The NED values correlated strongly with the ability of an RNA to induce network formation.
source: The NED values correlated strongly with the ability of an RNA to induce network formation and clearly separated the two groups of RNAs with respect to network formation (Figure 3F).
evidence: Stated observation supported by Figure 3F showing significant difference

claim: The majority of network-forming RNAs had NED values higher than 0.280.
source: The majority of network-forming RNAs had NED values that were higher than 0.280, whereas the majority of sphere-forming RNAs had NED values lower than 0.265.
evidence: Stated observation from NED analysis

claim: The majority of sphere-forming RNAs had NED values lower than 0.265.
source: The majority of network-forming RNAs had NED values that were higher than 0.280, whereas the majority of sphere-forming RNAs had NED values lower than 0.265.
evidence: Stated observation from NED analysis

claim: 19 out of 24 (79%) of the tested RNAs were predicted correctly with respect to their sphere- or network-forming abilities using NED values.
source: We found that 19/24 (79%) of the tested RNAs were predicted correctly with respect to their sphere- or network-forming abilities (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 4A, B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Stated result from validation experiment

claim: Large disordered regions of 3′UTRs determine network formation.
source: As the number of AU-rich elements in both groups is comparable (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A), the high success rate strongly suggests that LDRs of 3′UTRs determine network formation.
evidence: Inference from high prediction success rate and comparable AU-rich element numbers

claim: The TNFSF11 3′UTR mutant with stronger local structures has largely lost the ability for network formation.
source: The TNFSF11 3′UTR mutant has stronger local structures indicated by increased base-pairing and a lower NED value, and it has largely lost the ability for network formation (Figure 3H, I).
evidence: Stated observation from loss-of-function experiment shown in figures

claim: A high diversity of predicted structural conformations correlates with the extent of LDRs in RNAs and is associated with the formation of mesh-like condensates.
source: Taken together, these results support a model wherein a high diversity of predicted structural conformations correlates with the extent of LDRs in RNAs and is associated with the formation of mesh-like condensates.
evidence: Summary conclusion from NED analysis and experimental validation

claim: The minimum RNA concentration for network formation was 20 nM, observed for the CD47 and ELAVL1 3′UTRs.
source: The minimum RNA concentration for network formation was 20 nM. It was observed for the CD47 and ELAVL1 3′UTRs and corresponds to 27 and 32 ng/µl, respectively (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Stated observation from concentration-dependent experiments

claim: The minimum RNA concentration for network formation (20 nM) is higher than the mRNA concentration in the cytoplasm of mammalian cells, which was estimated to be 8 pM to 8 nM.
source: This is higher than the mRNA concentration in the cytoplasm of mammalian cells, which was estimated to be 8 pM to 8 nM (9.5 pg/µl to 9.5 ng/µl; see Materials and methods) (Chen et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2016; Maharana et al., 2018).
evidence: Comparison with literature values for cellular mRNA concentration

claim: Two different fluorescently labeled RNAs co-localize in the network.
source: Labeling of several pairs of RNAs with two different fluorescent dyes showed that they co-localize (Figure 4A).
evidence: Stated observation supported by Figure 4A showing co-localization

claim: Mixing suboptimal amounts of four network-forming RNAs together with FUS-TIS resulted in network formation, indicating that the different RNAs have an additive effect.
source: Furthermore, the mixing of suboptimal amounts of four network-forming RNAs, together with FUS-TIS, resulted in network formation, indicating that the different RNAs have an additive effect (Figure 4B).
evidence: Stated observation and inference supported by Figure 4B

claim: Mixing 10 mRNAs together with FUS-TIS only required 2 nM (0.7–3.2 ng/µl) of each mRNA which is substantially lower than the average mRNA expression in cells.
source: Importantly, mixing 10 mRNAs together with FUS-TIS only required 2 nM (0.7–3.2 ng/µl) of each mRNA which is substantially lower than the average mRNA expression in cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: Stated observation supported by Figure 4B

claim: The RNA concentrations used for the in vitro experiments are in a range that is physiologically relevant.
source: These data indicate that the RNA concentrations used for the in vitro experiments are in a range that is physiologically relevant.
evidence: Inference from comparison of experimental concentrations with cellular mRNA levels

claim: RNAs that are unable to induce networks are predicted to form strong local structures, meaning that they have a high propensity for intramolecular interactions.
source: We had observed that RNAs that are unable to induce networks are predicted to form strong local structures, meaning that they have a high propensity for intramolecular interactions (Figure 5A).
evidence: Stated observation from RNAfold predictions

claim: Network formation is caused by intermolecular RNA–RNA interactions mediated by the LDRs of mRNAs.
source: This led us to hypothesize that network formation is caused by intermolecular RNA–RNA interactions mediated by the LDRs of mRNAs (Figure 5B).
evidence: Stated hypothesis based on structure predictions

claim: Native gel electrophoresis showed the appearance of diverse RNA species with high molecular weight only with the network-forming RNAs.
source: We observed the appearance of diverse RNA species with high molecular weight only with the network-forming RNAs (Figure 5C).
evidence: Stated observation supported by Figure 5C showing native gel

claim: The observed smear in native gel is not due to degradation as the denaturing gel demonstrates that the used RNAs are intact.
source: The observed smear is not due to degradation as the denaturing gel demonstrates that the used RNAs are intact (Figure 5C).
evidence: Stated observation supported by denaturing gel in Figure 5C

claim: mRNAs with LDRs form higher-order RNA interactions in vitro.
source: This suggested that mRNAs with LDRs form higher-order RNA interactions in vitro.
evidence: Inference from native gel electrophoresis results

claim: Addition of two predominantly structured 3′UTRs (TLR8 and MYC) generates sphere-like condensates.
source: A phase separation experiment with FUS-TIS confirmed that the addition of the two predominantly structured 3′UTRs (TLR8 and MYC) generates sphere-like condensates, whereas the addition of RNAs capable of forming a crosslinked RNA network (D1-TLR8-D2 and D1-MYC-D2), which we call an RNA matrix, induces formation of mesh-like FUS-TIS condensates (Figure 5F).
evidence: Stated observation supported by Figure 5F

claim: Addition of RNAs capable of forming a crosslinked RNA network (D1-TLR8-D2 and D1-MYC-D2) induces formation of mesh-like FUS-TIS condensates.
source: A phase separation experiment with FUS-TIS confirmed that the addition of the two predominantly structured 3′UTRs (TLR8 and MYC) generates sphere-like condensates, whereas the addition of RNAs capable of forming a crosslinked RNA network (D1-TLR8-D2 and D1-MYC-D2), which we call an RNA matrix, induces formation of mesh-like FUS-TIS condensates (Figure 5F).
evidence: Stated observation supported by Figure 5F

claim: An extensive, multivalent RNA interaction network can drive the formation of mesh-like condensates.
source: Taken together, this in vitro reconstitution experiment demonstrated that an extensive, multivalent RNA interaction network can drive the formation of mesh-like condensates.
evidence: Summary conclusion from in vitro reconstitution with engineered RNAs

claim: In the presence of all required elements (SUMO-SIM fused to MS2 coat protein, TLR8 and MYC 3′UTRs fused to MS2-binding sites, and the presence of the dimerization elements D1 and D2 in the RNAs), mesh-like condensate formation was observed in vivo.
source: In the presence of all the required elements (SUMO-SIM fused to MS2 coat protein, TLR8 and MYC 3′UTRs fused to MS2-binding sites, and the presence of the dimerization elements D1 and D2 in the RNAs), we observed mesh-like condensate formation in vivo, indicating that we are able to reconstitute mesh-like condensates in living cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: Stated observation supported by Figure 6A

claim: Omission of MS2-binding sites or the MS2 coat protein prevents recruitment of the mRNAs to the multivalent protein and completely prevents the formation of mesh-like condensates.
source: Omission of MS2-binding sites or the MS2 coat protein prevents recruitment of the mRNAs to the multivalent protein and completely prevents the formation of mesh-like condensates, indicating that RNA is absolutely required for mesh-like condensate formation (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: Stated observation supported by Figures 6C and 6D

claim: RNA is absolutely required for mesh-like condensate formation.
source: Omission of MS2-binding sites or the MS2 coat protein prevents recruitment of the mRNAs to the multivalent protein and completely prevents the formation of mesh-like condensates, indicating that RNA is absolutely required for mesh-like condensate formation (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: Inference from omission experiments shown in Figures 6C and 6D

claim: Omission of the two RNA dimerization elements from the system still allows recruitment of the RNAs to the multivalent protein but forms sphere-like condensates in the majority of cases.
source: Omission of the two RNA dimerization elements from the system still allows recruitment of the RNAs to the multivalent protein. As the RNAs are able to dimerize, they generate mesh-like condensates in a few cases, but form sphere-like condensates in the majority of cases (Figure 6B, E).
evidence: Stated observation supported by Figures 6B and 6E

claim: The presence of RNA dimerization elements that allow the generation of an extensive RNA interaction network substantially increases formation of mesh-like condensates in living cells.
source: However, the presence of RNA dimerization elements that allow the generation of an extensive RNA interaction network that interacts with a multivalent protein substantially increases formation of mesh-like condensates in living cells (Figure 6A, E).
evidence: Stated observation supported by Figures 6A and 6E showing quantification

claim: Phase separation of an RNA-binding protein, together with mostly structured RNAs, predominantly generates sphere-like condensates.
source: These in vivo reconstitution experiments confirm that phase separation of an RNA-binding protein, together with mostly structured RNAs, predominantly generates sphere-like condensates, whereas phase separation of the same RNA-binding protein bound to RNAs with an ability to generate an extensive interaction network form mesh-like condensates in living cells.
evidence: Summary conclusion from in vivo reconstitution experiments

claim: Phase separation of the same RNA-binding protein bound to RNAs with an ability to generate an extensive interaction network form mesh-like condensates in living cells.
source: These in vivo reconstitution experiments confirm that phase separation of an RNA-binding protein, together with mostly structured RNAs, predominantly generates sphere-like condensates, whereas phase separation of the same RNA-binding protein bound to RNAs with an ability to generate an extensive interaction network form mesh-like condensates in living cells.
evidence: Summary conclusion from in vivo reconstitution experiments

claim: mRNAs with several AU-rich elements in their 3′UTRs have longer 3′UTRs.
source: Transcriptome-wide analyses showed that mRNAs with several AU-rich elements in their 3′UTRs have longer 3′UTRs and higher NED values (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Stated observation from transcriptome-wide analysis shown in figures

claim: mRNAs with several AU-rich elements in their 3′UTRs have higher NED values.
source: Transcriptome-wide analyses showed that mRNAs with several AU-rich elements in their 3′UTRs have longer 3′UTRs and higher NED values (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Stated observation from transcriptome-wide analysis shown in figures

claim: HuR targets have longer 3′UTRs.
source: Analyzing HuR PAR-CLIP data showed that HuR targets also have longer 3′UTRs and higher NED values (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: Stated observation from PAR-CLIP data analysis shown in figures

claim: HuR targets have higher NED values.
source: Analyzing HuR PAR-CLIP data showed that HuR targets also have longer 3′UTRs and higher NED values (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: Stated observation from PAR-CLIP data analysis shown in figures

claim: The RRM1/2 of HuR in the context of two multivalent domains (TIS11B N/C-terminus or FUS-IDR) was sufficient for the generation of mesh-like condensates.
source: In the context of two multivalent domains (TIS11B N/C-terminus or FUS-IDR), the RRM1/2 of HuR was sufficient for the generation of mesh-like condensates (Figure 6F, G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Stated observation supported by figures showing HuR chimeric proteins

claim: Several chimeric proteins that consist of multivalent domains paired with RBDs that bind to RNA matrix-forming RNAs can form mesh-like condensates in cells.
source: Taken together, we showed that several chimeric proteins that consist of multivalent domains that are paired with RBDs that bind to RNA matrix-forming RNAs can form mesh-like condensates in cells (Table 1).
evidence: Summary conclusion supported by Table 1 showing multiple chimeric proteins

claim: Condensates that contain the predominantly structured 3′UTR of TLR8 fully fuse within 90 s.
source: As expected, the condensates that contain the predominantly structured 3′UTR of TLR8 fully fuse within 90 s (Figure 7A).
evidence: Stated observation supported by Figure 7A showing time-lapse imaging

claim: When two condensates that contain RNAs with LDRs, such as the 3′UTR of CD47, come into contact, they largely retain their shape and do not fully mix.
source: In contrast, when two condensates that contain RNAs with LDRs, such as the 3′UTR of CD47, come into contact, they largely retain their shape and do not fully mix (Figure 7B).
evidence: Stated observation supported by Figure 7B showing time-lapse imaging

claim: Two condensates containing RNAs with LDRs connect at the contact sites, enabling linkage of individual condensates and allowing them to grow into large assemblies with irregular shapes.
source: However, the two condensates connect at the contact sites; this enables linkage of individual condensates and allows them to grow into large assemblies with irregular shapes (Figure 7C).
evidence: Stated observation supported by Figure 7C showing time-lapse imaging

claim: Despite the filamentous condensate shape the protein components are still highly mobile as shown by FRAP experiments performed at 2 and 16 hr after mixing.
source: It is worth pointing out that despite the filamentous condensate shape the protein components are still highly mobile as was shown by FRAP experiments performed at 2 and 16 hr after mixing (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Stated observation supported by FRAP data in figures

claim: The distribution of sphere-forming mRNAs is relatively uniform in the FUS-TIS condensates.
source: We observed that the distribution of sphere-forming mRNAs is relatively uniform in the FUS-TIS condensates (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Stated observation supported by high-resolution imaging in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A

claim: Network-forming mRNAs are unevenly distributed and generate an underlying scaffold for the phase-separated protein that resembles a skeleton.
source: In contrast, the network-forming mRNAs are unevenly distributed and generate an underlying scaffold for the phase-separated protein that resembles a skeleton (Figure 7D).
evidence: Stated observation supported by high-resolution imaging in Figure 7D

claim: Sphere-forming mRNAs are mobile and exchange with their environment.
source: We observed indeed fast fluorescence recovery of sphere-forming mRNAs, including TLR8 and MYC, suggesting that they are highly mobile within the condensates (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Stated observation supported by FRAP data in figures

claim: Network-forming mRNAs of various lengths showed no fluorescence recovery.
source: In contrast, network-forming mRNAs of various lengths showed no fluorescence recovery (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), which supports the notion that these mRNAs act as skeleton or underlying RNA matrix for mesh-like condensates.
evidence: Stated observation supported by FRAP data in figures

claim: Network-forming mRNAs act as skeleton or underlying RNA matrix for mesh-like condensates.
source: In contrast, network-forming mRNAs of various lengths showed no fluorescence recovery (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), which supports the notion that these mRNAs act as skeleton or underlying RNA matrix for mesh-like condensates.
evidence: Inference from FRAP data showing no recovery for network-forming RNAs

claim: Multivalent RNA–RNA interactions drive the formation of mesh-like condensates.
source: We found that multivalent RNA–RNA interactions drive the formation of mesh-like condensates.
evidence: Summary conclusion from reconstitution experiments

claim: Both mesh-like and sphere-like condensates contain RNAs, but they contain different kinds of RNAs.
source: This indicates that both mesh-like and sphere-like condensates contain RNAs, but they contain different kinds of RNAs.
evidence: Inference from in vitro experiments showing equal recruitment but different morphologies

claim: The characteristic FRAP behavior with dynamic protein components and non-dynamic RNA components was observed in naturally occurring mesh-like L-bodies in frog oocytes.
source: Importantly, the characteristic FRAP behavior with dynamic protein components and non-dynamic RNA components was not only observed in our in vitro reconstitution experiments of mesh-like condensates, but also in the naturally occurring mesh-like L-bodies in frog oocytes (Neil et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature on L-bodies

claim: A large fraction of 3′UTRs has high RNA multivalency.
source: Our results further indicate that a large fraction of 3′UTRs has high RNA multivalency.
evidence: Inference from transcriptome-wide analysis of NED values

claim: The extent of RNA multivalency can be tested experimentally through native RNA gel analysis.
source: Our results show that the extent of RNA multivalency can be tested experimentally through native RNA gel analysis (Figure 5C, E).
evidence: Stated conclusion supported by native gel data in figures

claim: The multivalent 3′UTRs have a high propensity to form pervasive intermolecular interactions.
source: The multivalent 3′UTRs have a high propensity to form pervasive intermolecular interactions.
evidence: Stated conclusion from native gel and phase separation experiments

claim: The formation of a multivalent RNA interaction network is an emergent property of unstructured mRNA.
source: As this feature correlates with 'unstructured-ness' of the RNA, our observations suggest that the formation of a multivalent RNA interaction network is an emergent property of unstructured mRNA.
evidence: Inference from correlation between NED values and network formation

claim: The most important RNA feature to induce formation of mesh-like condensates is their capacity for pervasive intermolecular RNA–RNA interactions.
source: The most important RNA feature to induce formation of mesh-like condensates is their capacity for pervasive intermolecular RNA–RNA interactions.
evidence: Summary conclusion from all RNA experiments

claim: Predominantly structured RNAs that form extensive intermolecular interactions are able to form mesh-like condensates.
source: This means that predominantly structured RNAs that are somehow able to form extensive intermolecular interactions are also able to form mesh-like condensates. This was revealed by our in vivo reconstitution experiment where known RNA dimerization motifs that are mostly structured but that form a pervasive RNA matrix through multivalent RNA–RNA interactions are sufficient for mesh-like condensate formation in the presence of a multivalent RNA-binding protein (Figure 6).
evidence: Stated conclusion from in vivo reconstitution with dimerization elements

claim: The target mRNAs of TIS11B have higher NED values than 3′UTRs without AU-rich elements.
source: We found that the target mRNAs of TIS11B – which are characterized by the presence of multiple AU-rich elements in their 3′UTRs – have higher NED values than 3′UTRs without AU-rich elements (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Stated observation from transcriptome-wide analysis shown in figures

claim: mRNAs that are enriched in TIS granules are less structured and have a higher tendency to form multivalent RNA–RNA interactions.
source: This predicts that mRNAs that are enriched in TIS granules are less structured and have a higher tendency to form multivalent RNA–RNA interactions, thus making it likely that an underlying RNA matrix causes the mesh-like morphology of TIS granules.
evidence: Inference from NED analysis of TIS11B target mRNAs

claim: 3′UTRs may fulfill roles as structural elements for cytoplasmic RNA granules.
source: Our data suggest that, in addition to acting as information templates for protein synthesis, mRNAs and, in particular, 3′UTRs may further fulfill roles as structural elements for cytoplasmic RNA granules.
evidence: Inference from the scaffolding role of 3'UTRs demonstrated in the study

claim: Both 3′UTRs and lncRNAs have a similar AU-content and hexamer composition that differs substantially from the coding region.
source: Both 3′UTRs and lncRNAs have a similar AU-content and hexamer composition that differs substantially from the coding region. This finding provides further support for the scaffolding role of 3′UTRs because a higher AU-content is associated with decreased RNA structure and higher RNA flexibility (Niazi and Valadkhan, 2012).
evidence: Stated observation with citation supporting the connection to RNA flexibility

claim: A higher AU-content is associated with decreased RNA structure and higher RNA flexibility.
source: This finding provides further support for the scaffolding role of 3′UTRs because a higher AU-content is associated with decreased RNA structure and higher RNA flexibility (Niazi and Valadkhan, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Interacting 3′UTRs may scaffold additional cytoplasmic membraneless compartments, possibly on other membrane surfaces or on the cytoskeleton.
source: Therefore, it is likely that interacting 3′UTRs do not only act as RNA matrix for TIS granules and L-bodies, but may also scaffold additional cytoplasmic membraneless compartments, possibly on other membrane surfaces or on the cytoskeleton (Smith et al., 2020; Béthune et al., 2019).
evidence: Speculation based on findings with TIS granules and L-bodies, supported by citations

claim: Formation of filamentous and mesh-like condensates is not restricted to the chimeric RNA-binding proteins used in this study but was also observed by others.
source: Formation of filamentous and mesh-like condensates is not restricted to the chimeric RNA-binding proteins used here but was also observed by others (Lin et al., 2015; Boeynaems et al., 2019; Smith et al., 2020; Neil et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The mixing of a PR30 peptide with two homopolymeric RNA species with perfect base-pairing capabilities (poly-rA plus poly-rU) induced formation of filamentous condensates.
source: For example, the mixing of a PR30 peptide with two homopolymeric RNA species with perfect base-pairing capabilities (poly-rA plus poly-rU) induced formation of filamentous condensates (Boeynaems et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: PR30 condensates showed little fluorescent recovery upon FRAP, suggesting that physical cross-linking of the base-paired RNA structures and the PR molecules arrests phase separation.
source: The PR30 condensates showed little fluorescent recovery upon FRAP, thus, suggesting that physical cross-linking of the base-paired RNA structures and the PR molecules arrests phase separation (Boeynaems et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Some filamentous condensates are solid, whereas others are dynamic, and their material properties are regulated by the extent and strength of RNA–protein and RNA–RNA interactions.
source: These observations indicate that some filamentous condensates are solid, whereas others are dynamic, and their material properties are regulated by the extent and strength of RNA–protein and RNA–RNA interactions (Ferrandon et al., 1997; Jambor et al., 2011; Trcek et al., 2015; Van Treeck et al., 2018; Trcek et al., 2020).
evidence: Inference from comparison of different systems, supported by citations

claim: Mesh-like condensates have a larger surface to volume ratio compared to spherical condensates.
source: Surface tension enforces a low surface to volume ratio for liquid-like spheres (Hyman et al., 2014). In contrast, mesh-like condensates have a larger surface to volume ratio.
evidence: Stated comparison based on geometric principles

claim: The large surface to volume ratio of mesh-like condensates gives them an advantage for reactions that occur on their surface.
source: This gives them an advantage for reactions that occur on their surface.
evidence: Inference from geometric properties

claim: The mesh-like shape of the TIS granule network is necessary for its function during translation of membrane proteins.
source: Our previous data suggests that the mesh-like shape of the TIS granule network is necessary for its function during translation of membrane proteins.
evidence: Stated inference from previous work

claim: Translation in the TIGER domain enables protein complex formation of membrane proteins and promotes their trafficking to the plasma membrane.
source: We showed previously that translation in the TIGER domain enables protein complex formation of membrane proteins and promotes their trafficking to the plasma membrane (Ma and Mayr, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: One potential biological implication for intermolecular mRNA–mRNA interactions in TIS granules could be to facilitate co-translational protein complex assembly.
source: One potential biological implication for intermolecular mRNA–mRNA interactions in TIS granules could be to facilitate co-translational protein complex assembly.
evidence: Stated as speculation about biological function

claim: The majority of protein complexes form co-translationally in yeast.
source: Although the majority of protein complexes form co-translationally in yeast (Shiber et al., 2018), it is unclear how the protein subunits come into proximity.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The physical interaction between LDRs in 3′UTRs may provide the necessary proximity of two translating ribosomes and their nascent peptide chains to promote complex assembly.
source: It is possible that the physical interaction between LDRs in 3′UTRs provides the necessary proximity of two translating ribosomes and their nascent peptide chains to promote complex assembly (Shiber et al., 2018; Mayr, 2018).
evidence: Stated as speculation with supporting citations

claim: The generation of mesh-like networks – either lipid membrane-enclosed or membraneless – is conceptually similar.
source: We noticed that the generation of mesh-like networks – either lipid membrane-enclosed or membraneless – is conceptually similar.
evidence: Stated observation from comparison

claim: Mesh-like condensates with dynamic protein components are generated from the interplay of two forces: one force promotes fusion driven by surface tension, and the other force prevents full fusion provided by the underlying RNA matrix.
source: Our model proposes that mesh-like condensates with dynamic protein components are generated from the interplay of two forces (Figure 7E). One force promotes fusion and is driven by the surface tension of the liquid condensates. The other force prevents full fusion and is provided by the underlying RNA matrix that forms a semirigid skeleton and only allows fusion of the condensates at the contact sites.
evidence: Stated model supported by experimental observations and Figure 7E

claim: The interplay of two antagonistic forces was observed upon in vitro reconstitution of the membrane-enclosed tubular ER network.
source: Such interplay of two antagonistic forces was also observed upon in vitro reconstitution of the membrane-enclosed tubular ER network (Powers et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Membrane-enclosed and membraneless network structures result from the balance of two opposing forces.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that membrane-enclosed and membraneless network structures result from the balance of two opposing forces.
evidence: Inference from comparison with ER network formation

claim: The network structure and morphogenesis of the tubular ER that is generated by proteins and lipids can be mimicked by phase-separated condensates formed by protein and RNA.
source: Here, we found that the network structure and morphogenesis of the tubular ER that is generated by proteins and lipids can be mimicked by phase-separated condensates formed by protein and RNA.
evidence: Summary conclusion from comparison with ER network

claim: Dynamic subcellular structures with complex shapes can be generated through phase separation without the need for lipid membranes.
source: Our work showed that dynamic subcellular structures with complex shapes can be generated through phase separation without the need for lipid membranes.
evidence: Summary conclusion from the entire study
